worst_places.after:
Three mitigations:

1. **Use an accumulator.** Convert tail-recursive patterns to accumulate a result, as in `Repeat` above. Each step then does less re-computation.
2. **Cap the depth you actually need.** Don't try to model arbitrary depth. `DeepPartial` implementations often just accept that they hit limits beyond ~10-15 levels of nesting, which is rarely a real-world concern.
3. **Break the cycle with a generic reference.** For true circular references in *runtime* object graphs — parent/child nodes pointing at each other — `type Node<T> = { value: T; parent?: Node<T> }` is fine. The recursion there is driven by actual nesting depth, not by a self-referential type with no base case.

worst_places.after:
Наивная версия выше упускает три крайних случая JSON-сериализации — их стоит упомянуть на интервью.

1. **`undefined` ведёт себя по-разному в объектах и массивах.** Свойство со значением `undefined` полностью выпадает из результата. А элемент массива со значением `undefined` превращается в `null`, а не убирается. `Serializable<T>` в текущем виде этого различия не делает.
2. **`Map` и `Set` теряют всё содержимое.** Они сериализуются в `{}` и `[]` соответственно, если не реализуют собственный `toJSON()`. Эта версия их вообще не учитывает.
3. **Циклические ссылки падают в рантайме** с `TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON`. Обнаружить это заранее на уровне типов нельзя: структурная система типов TypeScript видит только форму объекта, но не его идентичность.

worst_places.quote: Common pitfall: assuming a multi-site generic parameter resolves to whatever type the *first* argument happens to be, then being confused when an unrelated second argument silently widens the whole inferred type to a union, breaking downstream code that assumed a single concrete type — when a function genuinely needs both parameters to share one exact type rather than allowing this union-widening behavior, the fix is usually adding an explicit second type parameter constrained to the first (`function strict<T, U extends T>(a: T, b: U)`) rather than relying on default inference to enforce sameness it was never designed to enforce.

patterns: THE dominant pattern, and the one fix worth making: the bank is two different documents stitched together at typescript-q-45, and the seam is mechanical. Junior + middle (q-1..q-44) average 18-20 words per sentence in en / 15-17 in ru, with 21-23% / 11-14% of sentences over the limit. Senior + advanced (q-45..q-88) jump to 39-42 words per sentence in en / 35-39 in ru, with 69-75% / 57-66% over the limit. Nothing about the subject matter requires this: q-13 explains the `never` bottom type in 18-word sentences, while q-47 explains variance in 40-word ones. The seam is not gradual — it lands exactly on the difficulty boundary, which means it is an authoring-mode artifact, not a consequence of depth.

Inside that seam, the single most repeated defect is the closing 'Common pitfall' / 'Частая ловушка' paragraph collapsing into one sentence. Junior/middle pitfalls are 2.3-2.5 sentences averaging 35-39 words total; senior/advanced pitfalls are 1.5-1.8 sentences averaging 66-73 words, with the longest sentence in the paragraph averaging 53-59 words. The recipe is always the same: 'Common pitfall: <gerund>ing X, then being confused when Y — <em-dash> the fix is Z rather than W.' All 44 senior/advanced entries follow it. Splitting that one paragraph per entry into 3-4 sentences would fix roughly a third of the bank's total long-sentence count without touching a single technical claim.

A secondary but trust-damaging pattern: unedited drafting artifacts survive in three entries, all in the senior/advanced tier, all of the form '... actually <the opposite>'. typescript-q-82 reverses its own explanation of `Exact<T, Shape>` mid-sentence (both locales); typescript-q-49's code comment says a `const` literal is 'still string ... actually "red" for const' (en only — ru was cleaned); typescript-q-68 writes '// Error: Object literal may only specify known properties... actually here:' before quoting the real diagnostic (both locales). These are cheap to fix and they are the only places in 35k words where the text is actually wrong rather than merely long.

Deferral leads. Several senior/advanced entries open by pointing at other entries instead of answering: 'This combines three mechanisms covered separately elsewhere' (q-61), 'All four are built on the same core mechanism' (q-53), 'These utility types build on the basics (Partial/Pick/Omit)' (q-23). In a bank whose entries are read standalone and out of order, a lead that references sibling entries spends the highest-value sentence in the answer on nothing.
notes: What this bank does right, and should become the style guide's positive examples: (1) every answer has the same three-part skeleton — one-paragraph direct answer, bolded mini-sections each paired with a 5-8 line code block, closing 'Common pitfall' that states the actual misconception rather than recapping; theory_walls is 0 in both locales, which no other shape achieves. (2) On rubric E for type-level code it is genuinely strong: ~25% of code blocks quote a real compiler diagnostic and another ~22% annotate the inferred type inline, including exact TS error codes (q-84 `error TS1262`, q-75/81/83 `error TS2589`) and full messages (q-54's `Argument of type '{ kind: "triangle"; ... }' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'`, q-71's `this`-context error). Examples are self-contained and narrow — median code line is 27 chars, only 1.5-2% of junior/middle lines exceed 80. (3) Contrast pairs everywhere ('Without generics / With generics', 'Before TS 4.0 / After', BROKEN-vs-correct in q-71) give the reader a delta instead of a definition. Caveats on rubric E: advanced code blocks average 16.5 lines with 8.9% of lines over 80 chars (max 116, q-82's `ExactSelf` one-liner); a handful of 'Error' comments paraphrase the compiler rather than quote it (q-47, q-55); q-73's `onAny` snippet is a bare method body that dangles outside the class shown above it. On scoring: I treated each of the 88 entries as the real 'file' unit for rubric A, since a question bank is read entry-by-entry — that is why DI appears in the abbrev list (expanded in q-58, but used bare in q-67, where a reader arriving cold gets no expansion) while MFE, URI, HKT and AST do not (each is expanded inside its own entry). The verdict is targeted-fixes rather than systemic-refactor because the work is one repeatable operation applied to two known slots (lead sentence, closing pitfall paragraph) in the 44 senior/advanced entries, plus the ~6 one-off defects listed above — no restructuring, no content change, and the other 44 entries ship as they are.
